front: State the peak velocity/gradient thresholds for MILD, MODERATE, and SEVERE pulmonic stenosis.
back: Mild: peak velocity < 3 m/s (peak gradient < 36 mmHg). Moderate: 3–4 m/s (36–64 mmHg). Severe: > 4 m/s (> 64 mmHg).

front: Congenital syndromes associated with pulmonic stenosis?
back: Noonan syndrome (dysplastic PV), Williams syndrome (supravalvular PS + peripheral PS), congenital rubella (peripheral PS), tetralogy of Fallot (infundibular PS).

front: Give three echo criteria for SEVERE pulmonic regurgitation.
back: Steep CW deceleration slope (PR pressure half-time < 100 ms); vena contracta > 50% of PV annulus width by color; holodiastolic flow reversal in the pulmonary artery; RV dilation (chronic).

front: Most common cause of severe PR in adults?
back: Post-surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot with a transannular RVOT patch — creates chronic free PR. Also PAH-related annular dilation.

front: State the Mahan formula relating PA acceleration time to mean PA pressure.
back: Mean PAP (mmHg) ≈ 79 − 0.45 × AT (ms), where AT is the pulmonary flow acceleration time in the RVOT.

front: What pulmonary acceleration time indicates elevated mean PAP?
back: AT ≤ 100 ms suggests elevated mean PAP. Normal AT ≥ 130 ms. AT is measured from the onset of pulmonary ejection to peak velocity on PW Doppler in the RVOT.

front: Compare pulmonic valve M-mode findings in pulmonic stenosis vs severe pulmonary hypertension.
back: PS: exaggerated prominent 'a'-wave, NO mid-systolic notching. Severe PAH: diminutive/absent 'a'-wave WITH mid-systolic notching ('flying-W sign'), from transient reversal of the RVOT–PA gradient due to poor PA compliance.
